children: Is Elon Musk's SpaceX
a buy, sell, or hold right now?
Seeking Alpha analysts
, and Daniel Jones weigh in.
Mike Zaccardi: I still think SpaceX

is attractive here. While the valuation remains questionable, sentiment is clearly extremely depressed. Investors should recall how strong the company's Q3 was, and while the midterms were a setback, a blue wave was expected. Technically, all eyes are now on the low near $105.
Michael Del Monte: Buy rating. SpaceX

is accelerating the expansion of its data center capacity to both internally develop Grok and rent excess compute capacity for high-margin revenue. I believe SpaceX may lean into its partnership with Intel
for inference capacity while expanding training capacity with Nvidia
GPUs, at least going into the emergence of Terafab.
SpaceX is also becoming a threat to the traditional telco service providers, with plans to rapidly expand its Starlink program for both broadband and direct-to-device cellular service.
Yiannis Zourmpanos: SpaceX's
infrastructure advantage remains impressive, but Anthropic's
contractual flexibility and potentially fading AI compute scarcity threaten current returns.
Daniel Jones: Since I last reaffirmed Space Exploration Technologies

as a Strong Sell back in early August, shares have skyrocketed 19.5%, while the S&P 500 is down 5.1%. This might seem to be a stunning rebuke to my bearish stance on the business. Newer data that has come out has shown that I was perhaps a bit overly pessimistic in my assessment of the business. But this doesn't change the fact that shares look rather pricey when you consider that growth appears limited in most of its operating segments.

This is not to say that there aren't positives about the company. In my previous article, I looked at each of its operating segments. I was particularly impressed by its Connectivity segment that had seen tremendous growth and was materially profitable. It continues to expand. The 13.6M consumer subscribers that it had at the end of the most recent quarter were well above the 7.2M reported a year earlier.

Unfortunately, monthly ARPU continues to fall, dropping from $83 last year to $69 this year. But that is a small price to pay for the overall expansion the business has experienced. Revenue shot up from $3.1B to $5.25B for this segment, and operating profits nearly doubled to $2.37B.

The company is also seeing growth elsewhere, but it's not exceptional by comparison. The one exception to this would be its Super Intelligence segment that includes AI infrastructure, Grok, and Twitter. The surge in revenue from $813M to $7.56B was phenomenal. We also saw modest expansion for its Space segment.

The problem is that shares are not exactly cheap. Management forecasted that first quarter revenue for 2027 could balloon to as much as $37B, with the lower end of that range hitting $33B. Annual recurring revenue by the end of this year should be around $100B. But even if the company achieves $40B in quarterly revenue, that would still make it trade at about 10.5 times sales. Assuming the same adjusted operating cash flow margin as what the company has captured so far in 2026, we would be looking at a price-to-operating-cash-flow multiple of 17.

That on its own is not crazy. But when you consider that growth opportunities from here are limited, especially with other players dominating in AI and AI infrastructure, the Space segment not really having phenomenal growth potential, and the Connectivity segment being the only real expansion driver, I really don't see a path forward to significant market beating potential over the long run.

Having said that, based on the developments management has achieved, I would say a less pessimistic stance on the business is justified compared to my previous rating. That's why I think calling it a Sell today is appropriate.
(Daniel Jones runs the SA investment newsletter Crude Value Insights.)
